<meta>This page follows the title page and serves as the epigraph for the treatise. It features a passage from the Roman Stoic philosopher Seneca the Younger's work "Naturales Quaestiones" (Natural Questions), written around 65 AD. This choice of text sets a philosophical and reverent tone for Cohausen's scientific inquiry, framing the study of light and "phosphors" as a gradual initiation into the sacred mysteries of the natural world.</meta>

The world is a small thing, unless it contains within it something for the whole world to seek. Certain sacred mysteries are not revealed all at once: Eleusis <note>The site of the Eleusinian Mysteries in ancient Greece, famous for secret religious rites where knowledge was revealed in stages to the "initiated."</note> keeps back things to show to those who return to visit. Nature does not reveal her mysteries all at once. We believe ourselves to be initiated: yet we linger only in her entryway <note>original: "vestibulo" — the porch or entrance hall of a Roman house or temple.</note>. Those secrets are not open indiscriminately, nor to everyone; they are withdrawn and shut away in the inner shrine. Of these, our age will see some things, and the age that follows us will see others. When, then, will these things be brought into our knowledge? Great discoveries come forth slowly, especially if our labor ceases.

You ask, what shall be the reward for this labor, than which there is none greater? To know Nature. For the study of this subject has nothing in it more beautiful—though it contains much that will be of future use—than the fact that it captivates man by its own magnificence, and is pursued not for profit, but for the sheer wonder of it.

->Seneca, *Natural Questions*<-

# PHYSICO-CHEMICAL DISSERTATION
## ON THE CAUSE OF LIGHT IN PHOSPHORS <note>The term "Phosphor" (from the Greek for "light-bearer") was used in this period to describe any substance—organic or mineral—that could emit light in the dark, including what we now call bioluminescence and phosphorescence.</note>
->SUMMARY<-

# INTRODUCTION. <note>original: "ISAGOGE." A Greek term commonly used in academic texts to denote a formal introduction or scholarly entry into a subject.</note>

§. I. *The origin of primordial light is explained.*
§. II. *Light is established both in the elements and in composite bodies.* <note>original: "elementatis corporibus." In early modern science, "elements" were the simple building blocks (like air or water), while "composite bodies" were complex substances formed from their mixture.</note>
§. III. *The nature of light and fire is explained according to the hypotheses of modern authors.* <note>original: "Recentiorum." This refers to "the Moderns," likely including figures like Descartes, Newton, or Boyle, as opposed to "the Ancients" like Aristotle.</note>

# PART I.

## Concerning the natural Phosphors of the animal & vegetable Kingdoms.

### SUBSECTION I.
### Concerning the Phosphors of Animals.

§. I. *Concerning the light of Humans and its origin & cause.* <note>In the 17th and 18th centuries, scholars were fascinated by rare reports of "luminous" people whose skin or sweat allegedly glowed, often attributed to specific diets or illnesses.</note>

## INTRODUCTION TO LIGHT IN PHOSPHORS.

<margin>A 4</margin>

Some among them, however, believe that once this division had been accomplished by the light, the light itself utterly ceased and plainly perished, and that the Sun succeeded to its place, role, and office.

My reason for not subscribing to this latter postulate is the excellence of Light—that most noble creature to which the Creator himself gave the praise that "it was good." It is not probable that such a thing was then destroyed; rather, as others maintain, it is more likely that once the darkness was entirely conquered and pressed down toward the center, the light was contracted into that shining and most noble globe of the Sun, extraordinary in both its magnitude and form. This was done so that the more concentrated the light, the more effective it would be, casting its rays more powerfully. Furthermore, it was so that created Light—the closest image of divine glory proceeding from the <term>uncreated Unity</term> <note>A theological/philosophical term for God as the singular, eternal source of all being.</note>—might be poured out through a single point into all creatures. Thus, preserved within the Sun as if in its own dwelling place, it would be the author of all motion, light, and heat in the <term>sublunary world</term> <note>The physical realm beneath the moon, traditionally considered the area of change, growth, and decay.</note>. ### The nature of Light & Fire is explained according to the hypotheses of the Moderns.

## PHYSICO-CHEMICAL EXERCISE ON THE CAUSE

Light and fire differ in various ways—light from light, and fire from fire—both by reason of their origin and their effects. Light is destined for the birth and preservation of things; fire for death and ruin. Hence the **mechanism of the Universe** <note>original: *Universi machina*. A common 17th-century metaphor viewing the world as a complex, divinely-crafted clockwork or machine.</note> began from light, and will one day perish by fire. They seem indeed to agree in brightness, speed, subtlety, and the power of penetrating; yet they differ in their circumstances and their different mode of existing. Fire, for its own preservation, requires a **sulfurous fuel** <note>The author is likely referring to the alchemical principle of Sulfur, which was thought to be the principle of combustibility in all substances.</note>; light requires none, while illumination <note>original: *lumen*. In Latin philosophy, a distinction was often made between *lux* (the source of light) and *lumen* (the light radiating through a medium).</note> requires the continuous nourishment of light. 

Light is a most simple entity and signifies merely the very rapid motion of the particles of the **first element** <term>first element: In the Cartesian and alchemical physics of the time, the "first element" consisted of the finest, most agitated particles of matter that filled all space and formed the sun and stars.</term> within themselves—and specifically an expanded motion—from which come Heat and Illumination. The *Cartesians* <note>Followers of René Descartes (1596–1650), who theorized that light was a mechanical pressure transmitted through "globules" of the second element (the ether).</note> indeed prefer an impulse of the **second element** or of ethereal globules, caused by the most rapid matter of the first element; but for us, who profess *Chemical Philosophy*, it is more pleasing—following the lead of *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the foundation of alchemy (the Hermetic Art) is attributed.</note>—to derive light from the motion of the first element within itself, so that we may provide a clearer torch for more perceptible **chemical operations**. 

Fire, however, signifies that same motion of light, but collected and concentrated, acting within another thing—namely, within a heap of earthly particles following this motion of light. Hence, for parching, burning, or flaming fire, one should not conceive of a matter <meta>catchword: which [quæ]</meta>

Phosphorus prepared from urine <note>original: *Phosphorus ex Urinâ paratus*. In this substance, **phlogistic** <term>phlogistic: Relating to "phlogiston," a hypothetical fire-like element that 18th-century chemists believed was released during combustion.</term> particles—having been expanded and moved more rapidly, or, according to the **Cartesians** <note>Followers of the philosopher René Descartes.</note>, being still surrounded by **ethereal globules** <term>ethereal globules: In Cartesian physics, these were tiny, spherical particles of the "second element" that filled the universe and transmitted light through their motion.</term>—at the very least shine. However, when they are pushed extremely rapidly—or when they flow together more violently because the ethereal particles have been driven out—they catch fire. 

In its actual state, this phosphorus is cold due to the stillness of the phlogistic principle, or rather, the lesser motion of light within its constricted pores. Yet, it grows warm and breaks out into flame if those pores are dilated by rubbing, causing the luminous particles to be moved and strike against each other with extreme rapidity. Many chemical experiments prove the same thing: that the most vehement motion alone produces fire—not because that motion is itself fire, but because it is at least the instrument of it. Although without motion there would be neither fire nor heat, nor could they even be conceived of, **Plato** himself already recognized this very fact, as we gather from an elegant passage in the *Theaetetus*: 

*Fire and heat, which beget and govern other things, are themselves produced from motion* <note>original: *ἀπὸ τῆς φορᾶς* (apo tēs phoras)</note> *and friction; and this is motion itself.*

Likewise, no bodies are luminous without motion. The skin of a cat or a dog does not shine in the dark unless, through rubbing, the sulfurous **effluvia** <term>effluvia: Invisible vapors or particles believed to flow out of bodies, often used to explain smells or electrical effects.</term> of the skin and the luminous **animal spirit** <term>animal spirit: A "subtle fluid" once thought to circulate through the nerves to facilitate movement, sensation, and life functions.</term> itself are driven into a stronger state of agitation. Phosphorus substances themselves, when enclosed in vials, do not shine—even though the matter is luminous in its own right—because the particles are in a state of particular rest. They only begin to shine when motion is restored to them, either by the introduction of air or by the admission of light, depending on the specific nature of the **Phosphorus**. If this motion is completely removed—whether the mobile particles are suppressed or fixed in place—they cease to glow.

Therefore, just as concentrated light that is moved more forcefully produces fire, so **rarefied fire** <note>original: *ignis rarefactus*. Furthermore, when particles of light are restricted to a narrow space but not fully compacted, they generate heat or **invisible fire**. I shall explain this more clearly. Light and fire are, as it were, mutual co-causes for one another. They follow one another according to the various ways they are modified. Fiery motion stands as the author of that other movement—namely, the **luminous motion**, which is the swiftest of all movements in the Universe. In a single moment, it vibrates from the heavens to the earth, and from a lit torch it spreads across several miles.

Whether this conjecture will satisfy curious investigators of physical things, I greatly doubt, since daylight at least suffices for fish, as for other living creatures, to seek food; to do this, they are permitted to range from the dark floor of the sea (which is certainly not dark everywhere) to the regions of the upper waters illuminated by the sun. As for the fact that fish devour fish, this is rather an institution of nature, and it is abundantly compensated for by the inexhaustible fertility of the sea in the continuous propagation of myriads of fish of every species. 

And why would this benefit be granted only to the fish of the seas, and not also to the inhabitants of rivers, since these too need their food and have their own nocturnal ambushers? ## THE LIGHT OF THE SEA and of Fish is from Salt.

This will indeed seem a **paradox** <note>original: "paradoxum." In early modern science, a paradox was not an impossibility, but an opinion that went against common sense or established belief.</note> to many, which nevertheless is most true; and I shall show bit by bit that it is the foundation of the entirety of more **hidden philosophy** <note>original: "Philosophiæ arcanioris." This refers to natural philosophy—the precursor to modern science—specifically the "arcane" or chemical study of the hidden properties of matter.</note>. If you remove the salt from the sea, you will find nothing in it that shines. Sea water deprived of it no longer shines, nor do we observe the waters of the most rapid rivers—which lack salt—to shine, even if they are more strongly agitated by a massive fall or by the wheels of mills. Justly, therefore, that is held to be the cause of a thing which, when present, the thing is present, and when removed, the thing is taken away.

If you desire to behold light in salt, melt **sal ammoniac** <term>Sal armoniacum: ammonium chloride, often derived in this period from organic matter like soot or urine.</term> with **quicklime** <term>Calce viva: calcium oxide, a caustic substance produced by heating limestone.</term>. A fleeting urinous spirit will fly off; strike this hardened salt with a strong hammer at night, and it will reveal fire by its blow. The experiment is made easier if iron rods are encrusted with this salt melted in a **crucible** <note>original: "tigillo." A ceramic or metal container used for melting substances at high temperatures.</note>; these, when struck forcefully with a hammer, will give off fiery sparks. This experiment, at least regarding its preparation, was already known to the ancient **chemists** <note>original: "Chymistarum." Here referring to alchemists.</note>, who sought in this product a fusible or liquefiable salt for the **transmutation of metals**—I know not what—with vain labor; however, the light and fire manifested in it are recent... <note>The text breaks off mid-word (recen-) as it reaches the end of the page.</note>

Oh, what hidden things of nature Chemical Analysis <term>Analysis Chymica: the process of breaking down substances into their fundamental parts to understand their composition</term> reveals! A critic <term>momus: a fault-finder or mocker, named after the Greek god of mockery</term> might indeed laugh at these things and object that sea salt does not burn, and therefore it is not endowed with a sulfurous nature. A brilliant conclusion, indeed! <note>The author is being sarcastic here, mocking those who rely on surface-level observations rather than deep chemical study.</note> Listen to Becher’s response. <margin>Supplement III, or the Sandy Ore.</margin>

# PART I ON THE CAUSES OF PHOSPHORUS
<note>In this context, "phosphorus" refers to any substance that emits light without heat, rather than specifically the chemical element.</note>

...it would be permitted to make this suspect. For although some wish to call the nocturnal splendor of gems into doubt, and even **Boëtius de Boot** and **Johannes de Laet**—most famous examiners of precious stones—dismiss as fictitious and rashly claimed what they report about East Indian **Diamonds**, namely that they vibrate light and rays in the dark if handled by the rubbing of hands or clothes. However, that great Counselor of Nature, **Robert Boyle**, proved this to be true, not only through the testimony of eyewitnesses such as **Varthema**, **Garcia de Orta** (Chief Physician to the Viceroy of the Indies), and the Italian writer **Benvenuto Cellini**, but also by his own demonstration before the **Royal Society** at **Gresham College**.

<margin>Letter to Robert Moray, p. 124.</margin>

First, therefore, let that white horse of Scaliger from Calabria leap forward into our midst. Intended for use as a heavy cavalry horse <note>original: "Cataphracti"</note>, it was always seen to shoot out sparks when rubbed with a currycomb <note>a metal comb used for grooming horses</note> in the darkness. This motion is readily followed by the massive collection of sulfurous corpuscles <term>corpusculorum sulphureorum: tiny particles of sulfur, which early modern scientists believed was the primary "fuel" for fire and light in the body</term> present in this animal.

According to how this or that reasoning might take place depending on various <term>peristases: A Greek-derived term meaning "circumstances" or "surrounding conditions."</term>. Let the Reader be free to adhere to whichever opinion they please in a matter of such obscurity, since none has been or will be discovered that is exempt from all doubt.

It is a most difficult question by what benefit so many animals that see at night discern their objects. It is well known that wolves, goats, dormice, cats <note>original: "Æluros," from the Greek 'ailouros' for cat.</note>, and horses, whose eyes are <term>glaucous: A pale blue or greyish-green color, often referring to the reflective quality (tapetum lucidum) of an animal's eyes.</term>, as well as night-wandering birds, can see in the darkness. Indeed, even if the golden radiance of the Sun and its daughter, the most beautiful light of day, were primarily intended for human sight, there are nonetheless, and have been, those among men for whom the night was not entirely obscure. Tiberius <note>The Roman Emperor Tiberius (42 BC – AD 37), who was rumored to have the ability to see in the dark upon first waking.</note> saw everything as clearly by night as by day. The eyes of Marius and Sulla <note>Gaius Marius and Lucius Cornelius Sulla, rival Roman generals known for their keen, piercing gazes.</note> were sharp in the shadows. Concerning the philosopher Asclepiodorus, **historians** testify that he wrote and read at night without a lamp. This opinion seems quite plausible and probable on one hand, but on the other, it is beset by the greatest difficulties.

They explain it plausibly in this way: ethereal globules <term>ethereal globules: In the physics of René Descartes, these were tiny, hard particles of the 'second element' that filled all space; the transmission of light was described as the mechanical pressure or 'shove' of these globules.</term> are impelled by a spirit, almost fiery in nature <note>original: "spiritum quasi igneum"</note>, which animals emit from their eyes. They add a comparison. Light produced in this way and reflected from objects back toward the animal's eyes, with a specific modification, directs the animal toward the vision of those objects. This is not unlike how a blind man <note>The "blind man with a staff" is a famous analogy used by René Descartes in his *Dioptrics* (1637) to explain how light acts as a mechanical pressure transmitted through a medium.</note> discerns objects in his path by means of a staff; insofar as the motion of the staff is caused by the blind man himself, but when it is struck back by resisting bodies toward his hand with a certain modification, it is sufficient to allow him to identify them. This opinion, although dressed in new colors <note>meaning: updated with contemporary scientific language</note>, does not differ much from that of Hipparchus (as cited in Plutarch) or that of Plato. Just as objects, even when affected by light itself, are not brought to everyone's eyes indiscriminately, so—which was the other point we had to investigate—there will clearly be a need for a specific arrangement and internal structure in those creatures, so that they might serve to receive nocturnal rather than diurnal light. An example of this is the marvelous configuration of the eyes in the owl, and especially the notable **nictitating membrane** <note>original: *membrana nictatoria*; a translucent "third eyelid" found in some animals that can be drawn across the eye for protection and moisture while maintaining some visibility</note>, which is of a configuration and size clearly similar to what is seen in the eyes of goats—which, if we believe Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (AD 23–79), the Roman author of *Natural History*</note>, see no less by night than owls do. There is a supreme and more prominent clarity of the humors, especially the **vitreous humor** <term>humorum vitrei: the clear, gel-like substance that fills the eyeball behind the lens</term>; there is also a closer proximity of the **crystalline humor** <term>humoris cristallini: the lens of the eye, which focuses light</term> to the pupil. The eyes themselves are positioned deep inside, near the brain, whose size they almost exceed. Furthermore, they are immobile; they do not exhibit an elliptical shape like human eyes, nor a round one like those of other animals, but are like a globe hollowed out on both sides by a turner, with a circular series of bony portions, just as depicted by Severinus in his *Zootomy* <note>Marcus Aurelius Severinus (1580–1656), a pioneering Italian anatomist; his *Zootomia Democritaea* (1645) was one of the first works of comparative anatomy</note>.

No less worthy of consideration are the eyes of cats, which—because they greatly enjoy and make use of the nocturnal light that Helmont <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a Flemish physician and chemist who theorized that the moon provided a specific kind of light necessary for nocturnal vision</note> derives from the moon—their pupils...

Yet, he testifies that of all those he knows, none shine at night. Therefore, we do not consider it worthwhile to investigate the causes of things whose very existence is still in doubt.

Nevertheless, even though these accounts abound with fables, we shall not exclude from the category of existing things other plants that might perhaps shine. It may be that the plants themselves glow, or perhaps the air surrounding them—or rather a vapor, either peculiar to certain places or exhaling from the plants themselves—ignites like a *will-o'-the-wisp* <note>original: *ignis fatuus*, literally "foolish fire," referring to atmospheric ghost lights often seen over marshes or bogs.</note>. There is no logical contradiction in the idea that plants themselves can shine, especially since they are endowed with a more intimate life than minerals. They might possess an innate light, or they might naturally attract and then reflect the sun’s rays. For even in the seeds of **Vegetables**

However, the reason why natural phosphors are observed more frequently in the animal kingdom <note>original: *monarchiâ animali*</note> than in the vegetable may be because animal forms—having emerged from the secret treasures of heaven and the Sun—possess a great deal of the lucid-fire-like virtue <note>original: *virtutis lucido-igneæ*; a vitalistic energy associated with light and heat</note> drawn from them; hence, in the order of creation, they followed the Sun. Vegetables, however, preceded it <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis, where plants are created on the third day and the Sun on the fourth</note>. Hence, they do not attribute the beginnings of their ancient life to the Sun, but only to the luminous air or ether; because, lacking animal sensation and motion, they did not require that quantity of solar light for the motion of vegetation.

When this glue is finally consumed, solidity and firmness perish, and the final wasting of trees—decay—follows.

These are the final fates of the aging tree; from where, then, I ask, does that light come, now that the sulfur is already exhausted? Or perhaps, while the mixture of elements is dissolved through putrefaction and a separation of the principles occurs, does the vital soul of the wood <note>original: *vitalis ligni anima*</note>—or the ethereal formal principle—now on the very brink of flight, bid farewell to its dwelling with this final light? But this soul has long since broken out, departed, and escaped, unless it is still held back by some viscosity or oiliness of salt or sulfur...

<margin>Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*, 21.</margin>
Had the Roman Philosopher <note>Seneca the Younger (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Stoic philosopher whose works often touched on natural phenomena.</note> seen it, he would have recognized no true light in it, but at least a splendor. He says: *“There is a difference between splendor and light, since light has its own certain origin, while splendor shines with a borrowed one.”* <note>original: "Interest inquit inter splendorem & lucem, cum hæc certam originem habeat ac suam, ille niteat alieno."</note> By this decree, one would have to conclude that "light" exists in urine-based phosphorus <note>White phosphorus, which glows spontaneously upon exposure to air.</note>, while in the Bologna Stone there is only "splendor," since the latter shines by a borrowed light according to common opinion, while the former glows with its own. I apply to both what he adds next: *“Because this [splendor] is struck by a brightness coming from the outside, whoever stands in the way will immediately cast a thick shadow upon it; but that [light] is illustrious by its own radiance.”* <note>original: "Hic quia fulgore extrinsecus veniente percussus est, crassam illi statim umbram faciet, quisquis obstiterit, ille verò suo lumine illustris est."</note> Indeed, if you block the stone so that it cannot drink in the bright air—or at least an external splendor from a fire—it remains entirely in shadow. However, urine-based phosphorus needs only air—and not even bright air—which is why it is called the "aerial night-shiner" <note>original: *Noctiluca aëria*.</note>. We shall retain this name for the sake of distinction hereafter; as for the terms *radiance*, *light*, and *splendor*, we shall use them interchangeably, without heed for the petty disputes of the schoolmen <term>Schoolmen: Scholars of Medieval and Early Modern universities who obsessed over precise Aristotelian definitions.</term>.

...shines out. Although countless sulfurous subjects, even when **calcined** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air or oxygen to change its physical or chemical structure.</note> in the same way, do not exhibit a similar effect. Nothing, indeed, is easier to say than that the most subtle **matter of the first element** <term>first element: In the physics of René Descartes, the finest and most mobile matter (fire-matter) that fills the tiny spaces between larger particles.</term> enters the pores of the stone prepared in this way in a concentrated manner, and being held there for some time, produces light.

But how will this satisfy an investigator of physical things who does not merely stick to the surface? For it is a **begging of the question** <note>original: "petitio principii." A logical fallacy where the premise assumes the truth of the conclusion.</note>, and the same obscurity returns: why should this most subtle matter enter the calcined stone rather than the raw one? This theory requires the smallest pores, yet calcination—which induces a looser texture in things—shows that pores are more constricted in the raw stone than in the calcined one.

To this, if someone were to respond that light is not produced by the matter of the first element unless the **globules of the second element** <term>globules of the second element: In Cartesian physics, these are spherical particles (air-matter) that transmit light through their motion or pressure.</term> are driven through it; and that these are admitted more readily and abundantly within the pores of the calcined stone than within the raw one, he seems to say something, but not everything. For the same argument returns regarding other things that are equally calcined yet do not shine.

Not far from this opinion is that of the most celebrated ***Liceti*** <note>Fortunio Liceti (1577–1657), an Italian physician and philosopher who wrote a famous treatise on the Bologna Stone titled "Litotheoros."</note>, who established that a vaporous residue of illuminated air within the pores of the calcined stone is the cause of the light.

But *Van Helmont* <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a chemist and physician who bridged the gap between alchemy and modern chemistry.</note> has already sufficiently demonstrated that light is not immediately present in the air. And how could such **vaporous air** (by which I believe he meant air filled with vapors) be the subject of light—to which vapors are usually opposed—unless he perhaps thought they behaved like a flammable smoke, and just as smoke catches flame from fire, so this air draws light from light. To excuse the man as much as I can, I believe that by **vaporous** air he understood the sulfurous breaths remaining within the pores of the **calcined stone** <note>The Bologna Stone, a type of barite (barium sulfate) that phosphoresces after being heated, or "calcined."</note>. *Montalbano* <note>Ovidio Montalbani (1601–1671), a professor at Bologna who wrote extensively on the "Bologna Stone."</note> certainly assumed such things in it, because he posited that sulfurous and fiery **effluvia** <term>effluvia: Invisible outflows or particles emitted from a substance, a common explanation for physical phenomena in 17th-century science.</term> emerge from it; and due to their nature being related to light and fire, they are ignited by the surrounding light and "drink in" that light. What inconsistencies this emanation of effluvia from a luminous thing entails, we have already declared elsewhere. And so, the concepts of these distinguished men will hardly satisfy a **natural philosopher** <term>Physico: In this period, a "physicus" was a scholar who studied the laws of nature and the physical world.</term>.

The stone shines, but what **actual heat** <term>actual heat: Heat that can be felt by touch, as opposed to "potential" heat stored within a substance's nature.</term> might be hidden within it, I do not know. For **potential heat** is not sufficient, since anything that actually shines should also, according to such an opinion, be actually hot—whereas there are countless things that are potentially hot but do not shine. Therefore, this wonderful phenomenon of light must be explained in a far different way, and thus the nature of the **calcined stone** <note>The Bologna Stone, a form of barite that phosphoresces after being heated (calcined) with charcoal.</note> must first be investigated more deeply. We shall now see how this investigation has been conducted by the moderns.

It is a well-known postulate of more recent physics that *sulfur is the matrix of light*, and therefore whatever burns or shines participates in a sulfurous nature. Relying no doubt on this foundation, **Lemery** <note>Nicolas Lemery (1645–1715), an influential French chemist who sought to explain chemical reactions through the shape and motion of particles.</note> argues that sulfur—rendered more "exalted," mobile, and subtle by the calcination of the stone—is the cause of its light. Since no more plausible theory has appeared until now, many have subscribed to this view. This most expert man will therefore permit me to bring these points back for scrutiny, not out of a desire for contradiction, but out of a love for physical truth.

Thus, to uncover the nature of the light in the **Bologna Stone**, he established a comparison between this stone and the **aerial night-light** <note>original: "noctiluca aëria." This refers to the chemical element phosphorus, which had been recently discovered in the late 17th century and was known for glowing upon exposure to air.</note>. ...demonstrated. A great disparity must be observed here. It is not the nature of air to illuminate, but of light. Air can cause matter to release light if it holds some enclosed within, but it cannot cause matter to pour out light where it possesses none. The **noctiluca** <note>original: "noctiluca," meaning "night-shiner," a term used here for phosphorus.</note> does not shine because it receives light from the air, but because the light's action is merely mediated by it. Furthermore, there is a greater activity and energy in light than in air; hence the stone needs light rather than air for the expansion and movement of its coarser **sulfur** <note>In 17th-century chemistry, sulfur was considered the principle of inflammability and light.</note>. Because of its fixed **earthiness** <term>terrestreitas: A technical term for the solid, non-volatile parts of a substance that resist motion or fire.</term>, the stone can never be reduced to such a state—even with the addition of **combustible material** <term>rem cremabilem: Any substance capable of being burned.</term>—that it might catch fire from the air alone through motion, as the other substance does. 

Therefore, external light does not make the stone luminous because its sulfur is more "exalted" <term>exaltatum: An alchemical term for a substance that has been refined to increase its power or purity.</term> or purified from coarser parts (as **L'Emerius** <note>Nicolas Lemery (1645–1715), a prominent French chemist who wrote extensively on the chemistry of phosphorus.</note> supposes). Rather, it is because the stone lacks a sufficiently active internal light. Thus, it requires a stronger "mover" than air—namely, the matter of the **first element** <term>first element: In Cartesian physics, the finest and most mobile form of matter that constitutes light and fire.</term>, or an **ether** <term>ether: A subtle, fluid medium believed to fill the universe and transmit light waves.</term> that is already luminous. This ether, being most forcefully moved and impelled by light, stirs the ether within the stone into a similar motion, which is light itself. For as he himself freely concedes, not even all the air in the world is capable of moving the stone's particles rapidly enough to ignite them; which, by Hercules <note>original: "herculè," a common Latin exclamation used to emphasize the truth of a statement.</note>, does not prove their...

...exaltation and subtlety. On the contrary, **Urinary Phosphorus** <term>Phosphorus urinosus: Now known as white phosphorus, which was originally isolated from urine and glows spontaneously in the dark.</term> does not demand external light because it abounds with its own: that is, being already entirely volatile within itself, it possesses motion, for which a tiny bit of air—even unlit—is sufficient to excite and increase it, so that it shines. To be sure, this substance contains the formal principle of fire and light, participating heavily in a **rarefied** <term>rarefacto: thinned out or made less dense, which in 17th-century science increased a substance's activity.</term> and expanded **sulfur** <note>In early modern chemistry, "sulfur" referred to the principle of flammability and oily or fatty components of matter.</note>; and it is uniform throughout all its parts, even internal ones, which is why it shines and burns through its whole mass. 

The **Bologna Stone** <note>Lapis Bononiensis: A variety of barite that, after being heated with charcoal (calcined), exhibits phosphorescence—the ability to glow in the dark after exposure to light.</note>, however, is destitute of such abundance and energy of sulfur; it possesses at most certain residual sulfur particles adhering to its surface which are affected by light. Therefore, it is not "kindled" by light in the way a coal is by fire; for a coal contains inflammable sulfur as a material uniquely destined to sustain fire—the likes of which are not found in the **calcined stone** <term>lapide calcinato: A stone that has been purified or transformed by high heat.</term>. Hence, **Menzelius** <note>Christian Mentzel (1622–1701), a German physician and botanist who published works on the Bologna Stone.</note> proves by his own experience that the more the stone is purified and freed from sulfur, the more it shines.

This supposed **exaltation** <term>exaltatio: An alchemical term for the refinement or strengthening of a substance's properties.</term> and abundance of sulfur will more easily be refuted if we consider the phenomena that occur regarding the stone. Experience establishes that its "kindling" <note>original: "accensionem." Here used metaphorically for the stone being "charged" with light.</note> is scarcely possible unless the Sun is above the horizon, from which, nevertheless, light [is brought to] it...

## PART II: ON THE CAUSES IN PHOSPHORUS

...once kindled, it is again dissipated within a short time, which sufficiently proves the scarcity and more difficult movement of its **luminous sulfur** <note>In 17th-century chemistry, "sulfur" was considered the principle of flammability and light-bearing properties in all matter, not just the chemical element sulfur.</note>. Furthermore, it is clear from this with what certainty the cause of light is sought—whether from the abundance or the **exaltation** <term>exaltatione: The chemical process of refining or "raising" a substance to its most potent, active state.</term> of the sulfur. For there exist sulfurs far more subtle, exalted, and **rarefied** <term>rarefacta: Thinned out or made more "spirit-like," which was thought to increase the internal motion of particles.</term> in **distilled spirits** <note>original: "spiritibus alicoolisatis" — high-proof alcohol or rectified spirits.</note> and **essential oils** <note>original: "oleis æthereis" — volatile oils extracted from plants.</note>, which nevertheless do not shine at all, even though the internal motion of their particles is incomparably more intense than in the **light-bearing stone** <note>The Bologna Stone (*Lapis Bononiensis*).</note>.

The light of the **Sun** itself, when striking the stone directly, is so far from granting it greater light that it even partially deprives it of its glow—as experience witnesses and as a manifest sign shows. The "patient" <note>The substance receiving the action (the stone).</note> is not proportioned to such a powerful "agent" <note>The force acting upon the substance (the sun's rays).</note>, and the small amount of luminous sulfur is unable to resist such intense light; for in this same way, the Sun also extinguishes the light of a candle. 

However, on a less clear day, or when the Sun is already sinking toward its setting or covered by clouds, a lesser light acts upon the stone. This is because there is a greater proportion between the stone's weak sulfur and "lowered" rays than with "exalted" ones, and with fewer rays than with a great abundance of them. By contrast, the **aerial night-shiner** <term>Noctiluca aëria: A term for white phosphorus, which glows spontaneously and is highly flammable.</term> is—under certain conditions—terrifically inflamed by a sudden fire upon direct exposure to the Sun, which proves the presence of the most highly **exalted sulfur**.

I would grant that the **sulfur** <note>In early modern chemistry, "sulfur" was not just the element but a "principle" or "spirit" of flammability and light found within matter.</note> in the stone is "delicate," as the Author calls it, if by that term he understands it to be exceedingly weak. The very preparation of the stone contradicts the postulate of that most Excellent Man. I am aware that the sulfurs of minerals and metals are **exalted** <term>exaltari: Refined or brought to a higher state of potency through chemical processing.</term> by long-lasting fire. ### ON THE CAUSES OF PHOSPHORUS, PART II.

...indeed, in the inner parts of the stone, where **sulfur** <note>In this context, sulfur refers to the "combustible principle" thought to be present in minerals.</note> happens to remain, no light—nor even the capacity for receiving light—is observed. However, where the sulfur has ceased to be or has exited, there the light is able to enter once again. Furthermore, there is neither any argument nor any experiment that makes plausible that "tumbling and agitation" of sulfurous particles around the surface of the stone which that **Most Expert Man** <note>A polite but skeptical reference to the opposing theorist, likely a French scientist given the following quotes.</note> has established. **"These sulfurous particles,"** as he says, **"flying perpetually at the surface of the stone."** <note>original French: "Ces parties... sulphureuses voltigeantes perpetuellement à la superfice de la pierre."</note>

Would such a thing not require a perpetual emanation of **effluvia**? <term>effluvium: An invisible outflow of particles or "vapors" thought to travel from a substance to produce physical effects.</term> And from what source would that **calcined** stone have an inexhaustible fountain, or at least a discharge of **aporrhoeas** <term>aporrhoea: A technical term from Greek meaning a "flowing off" or streaming of atoms/particles.</term> lasting for so many years, as observations show us? The Author himself foresaw this "rock" <note>An idiom meaning a significant obstacle or logical pitfall.</note> well enough; therefore, to excuse the exhaustion of effluvia that would necessarily follow in a short time, he writes a new **paradox**: that while a few particles are dissipating, others fall back and re-enter their own pores to continually produce light, until all the sulfur has been evaporated. Let us hear those words, which are elegantly speculative: **"A little of it dissipates, but the greatest part falls back and re-enters into its pores to always produce light, until all the sulfur has evaporated."** <note>original French: "Il s'en dissipe quelque peu, mais la plus grande partie retombe & rentre dans ses pores pour produire toûjours de la lumiere, jusques à ce, que tout le soulfre se soit evaporé."</note>

### DISSERTATION ON LIGHT

Oh, what a wondrous vortex of **effluvia**! Who could imagine by what magnet or impulse the exhaled material particles of the shining stone return from its atmosphere to their own source? 

Fix those light-bearing **atoms** <note>In 17th-century natural philosophy, "atoms" referred to the smallest corpuscles or physical units of matter.</note> adhering to the surface of the **Bologna stone** <note>original: *lapis Bononiensis*. A variety of barite found near Bologna, famous for being the first known persistent phosphor.</note> to paper using **egg white**: this paper, when exposed to light, will catch it to be poured back out in the dark, not just once, but even by repeating the experiment many times. What exhalation of atoms from atoms, what tumbling, what return of atoms into atoms, or what dissipation of **sulfur** <note>Here used to mean the "inflammable principle" or chemical agent believed to cause light.</note> can be conceived of here? 

It is true: finally, after a period of three or four years through so many repeated exposures to daylight, the power of shining in the stone grows faint. This is not because the sulfur has been exhaled, or because it no longer returns into its pores, but because by that very frequent exposure and the impact of the **shining ether** <term>ether: A theoretical, weightless medium once believed to fill all space and transmit light waves.</term> it has either suffered a loss of those atoms adhering to the surface, or because by that frequent entry and exit of light, the **texture of the pores** has been so altered that the shining ether can no longer be received or properly moved within it hereafter—unless, as experience teaches, it recovers its original modification through a new **calcination** <term>calcination: The process of heating a mineral to high temperatures to change its physical or chemical state.</term>; yet never...

How shall we conceive of these things outside the action or presence of fire? Since sublunary fire <note>original: *ignis sublunaris*; fire as it exists on Earth, below the sphere of the moon, which early modern scientists distinguished from "celestial" fire.</note> is not an absolute being subsisting through itself, but only a motion of the particles of the <term>third element</term> <note>In Cartesian physics, the "third element" consists of the largest, least mobile particles that form solid bodies like planets and stones.</note> depending on the motion of the <term>first element</term> <note>The "first element" was thought to be an extremely fluid, fine matter that fills all gaps and makes up the sun and stars.</note>. Therefore, the matter seems to be explained by another way of occurring, which we have already partially hinted at above. Namely, this stone—through <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a mineral to high temperatures to purify it or change its state.</note> and especially through liberation from coarser sulfur—acquires such a texture (the nature of which I will explain soon) that it transmits a peculiarly modified ether. This ether easily obtains from the luminous ether surrounding it such an impulse and motion as the ether itself received from light (or the matter of the first element); and the stone retains this for a short time, even though that external source has already ceased to move. For just as the <term>celestial globules</term> <note>Part of Descartes' "second element," these were imagined as tiny spheres that transmitted light through pressure and vibration, like billiard balls.</note> **A**, moved by light, move the contiguous globules **B** and **C** with a similar motion so that they also shine, so the external ethereal globules surrounding the stone—which are already luminous—move the internal globules of that same stone (being also contiguous) in such a way that they shine likewise. This motion, however, because it is weak, soon fades away in the meantime, unless it receives a fresh impulse from light. Yet it does not fade as quickly as the motion of the ether illuminated by light [usually does] in the open and free atmosphere once the light is removed.

I think this is now evident enough, for in the previous chapter I established a parallelism between this substance and the <term>Bologna stone</term> <note>original: *lapidem Bononiensem*. # CHAPTER IV.

## Concerning the **<term>Flashing Night-Light</term>**, and the cause of its flashing.
<note>original: "Noctilucâ Fulgurante." Early scientists used the term "Noctiluca" (literally "night-shiner") to describe phosphorus before the element was fully categorized.</note>

This substance does not differ from the previously mentioned phosphorus in its material or nature, but only in its physical state and appearance. While the former appears in liquid form, this one appears as a solid; in both color and hardness, it resembles yellow amber—not entirely transparent, but somewhat dark. This variety was discovered by the aforementioned Daniel Krafft <note>Daniel Krafft (1642–1697) was a German chemist and merchant who purchased the secret of phosphorus from its discoverer, Hennig Brand, and famously demonstrated it to various European monarchs.</note>, and a singular occurrence led to this phenomenon of flashing.

He had enclosed the luminous matter he discovered in a **hermetically sealed** vial <note>A glass container made airtight by melting the neck shut, a technique named after Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note>, so that he might show it as a rarity at the court in Berlin to the most serene **Elector** <note>Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg (1620–1688), who was a significant patron of early modern science.</note>. When he arrived there and opened the glass, he took the material out and placed it on a piece of blue paper. Once the candles were removed, the substance shone like a **firefly** or **glow-worm** <note>original: "lampyridis sive Cicindulæ."</note> flying through the air on summer nights, much to the astonishment of the spectators, for at that time this "night-light" was not yet known. Afterward, the craftsman enclosed a grain of the material in an oblong glass tube, open at both ends, and sealed each opening with **sealing wax** <note>original: "cera hispanica," literally "Spanish wax," which was the standard material for sealing letters and vessels.</note>,

<meta>This page continues the theoretical explanation of the "flashing" phenomenon of phosphorus observed on the previous page. ### ON THE CAUSES OF PHOSPHORUS, PART II.

During the contraction <note>original: "systole"</note>, the sparkling light essentially collapses or is drawn back. For if this opposing motion did not exist, the light would simply emerge as a steady glow. The expansion <note>original: "diastole"</note> is caused by the effort of the luminous matter pushing outward, while the contraction is caused by the pressing force of the air pushing back against it.

<margin>Magdeburg Experiments, Book 7, Chapter 3. <note>A reference to Otto von Guericke’s 1672 work *Experimenta Nova Magdeburgica*, which discussed the vacuum and atmospheric pressure.</note></margin>
This flashing of the "night-light" <note>original: "noctilucae," a common early name for phosphorus</note> illustrates the doctrine of the most celebrated **Otto von Guericke** <note>Otto von Guericke (1602–1686) was a German physicist famous for his air pump and the "Magdeburg hemispheres" experiment.</note> regarding the twinkling of stars. He writes that stellar twinkling is nothing other than a very rapid rotation around their own centers, where the circles of the outer glowing parts are perceived to now contract, now extend, to a greater or lesser degree. A similar extension and contraction of glowing particles is observed in flashing phosphorus, when a small particle of the glowing-fiery matter, released by its natural motion or impulse, flashes and leaps out.

<margin>Collection 2, Secret 229. <note>Refers to a specific entry in a collection of scientific or medical "arcana" (secrets).</note></margin>
**Panarolus** <note>Domenico Panarolo (1587–1657) was an Italian physician and botanist who explored the relationship between light and life.</note> applies this motion of phosphorus to the human body. Through it, he attempts to explain the nature of life itself—which likewise consists of light—and the reciprocal rhythm of the heart and the arteries. However, the nature of vital light is quite different from the light found in phosphorus. For although vital light is rooted in a material or elemental mixture, and is sustained or destroyed by the elements, it is not elemental itself. Instead, it comes from a more noble lineage: the primordial light <note>original: "lucis primordialis," referring to the first light created at the beginning of the universe</note>, as we have already demonstrated elsewhere.

However, a proper but moderate calcination is required so that this luminous sulfur of the saltpeter, having been taken up by the **chalky body** <term>corpore cretaceo</term>, may expand further and move from its center toward the outer crust or rim. This is signaled by the aforementioned yellowish color, which is the only part that shines. Indeed, the interior parts of this substance do not glow, just like the **Bologna stone** <note>original: "lapidis Bononiensis." That process of extraction, or distillation, and a certain degree of calcination fixes the fiery-luminous particles—which are made mobile by light—onto the periphery of the chalk. It arranges them in such a way that the luminous ether is able to set them in motion.

I will speak briefly. **Michael Sendivogius** <note>A famous Polish alchemist (1566–1636) known for his work on the "food of life" in the air, which later scholars linked to the discovery of oxygen.</note>, sharper than the rest, teaches that the **celestial Sun** has a correspondence with the **central Sun** (thus he calls the **salt of the earth**) and possesses the power and virtue of distilling its rays into the earth. It is a great slowness of intellect to refer effects in nature, whose causes are more obscure, either to miracles or even sometimes to the tricks and illusions of the devil. If what Servius <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil's works</note> said is true: *Certainly, among the ancestors, altars were not set on fire, but they drew forth divine fire through prayers, which then kindled the altars.* This was rightly to be considered a miracle, just as there are unquestionable examples in the Holy Scriptures of such celestial fire consuming sacrifices. But whether the "fire-water" <note>original: *pyrophora*; literally "fire-bearer," referring to substances that ignite spontaneously</note> of the Maccabees was of such a divine nature is uncertain, for one might think that the method of its production, at least, does not exceed the forces of nature. Nor indeed should everything amazing that we read in those texts be relegated to the category of miracles.

# DISSERTATION ON LIGHTS

...if anything else, it is most worthy of consideration. It is metallic water <note>original: *Aqua metallica*. A common alchemical term for Mercury or Quicksilver.</note>, containing abundant light shut within it; however, this light does not shine out spontaneously unless it is aided by art. This is despite the fact that its body has a surface exceedingly well-suited for the reflection of light (for its countless tiny surfaces have the nature of a mirror; indeed, they are true mirrors reflecting the emerging rays of light not toward themselves, but outward in a dense mass), yet its interior remains most dark because it is so very dense.

<margin>Primarily in the *Memoirs* <note>The *Mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences*.</note>, Year 1701, p. 178.</margin>
The most celebrated Bernoulli <note>Johann Bernoulli (1667–1748), a Swiss mathematician who famously observed that a vacuum above mercury in a barometer would glow when shaken, a phenomenon known as "mercurial phosphorus."</note> gives testimony here and there in the *Acts of the Royal Academy of Sciences* that very pure mercury shone inside a glass tube sealed hermetically. That elegant Aphorism of Maxwell <note>William Maxwell (c. 1581–1641) was a Scottish physician who wrote on "magnetic medicine" and the idea of a universal vital spirit connecting all things.</note>, which tastes of a more recondite philosophy, also aims at this:

> *He who can lead light out of things by means of light, or multiply light with light, knows how to add the universal vital spirit to a particular vital spirit, and through this addition, to perform wonders.*

But what that "lucent salt" <note>original: *sal lucidum*</note> truly is, I have already stated, and a Philosopher will easily recognize it. There are those who, with volatile salt of urine, or of tartar, or even with animal Phosphorus, undertake great works concerning Mercury, so that they might lead its internal sulfur out to the surface; but we are sufficiently warned by the Adepts <note>In alchemical traditions, an "Adept" is an individual who has mastered the Great Work and discovered the Philosopher's Stone.</note> that these attempts are plainly futile. Granted, you might clothe quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*</note> with luminous salt of urine—will it therefore become the Phosphorus of the Philosophers, or the "lunaria" <note>A term often used for alchemical preparations associated with the moon or silver.</note>? Clothe a peasant in royal robes, will he turn out a king? Mix Phosphorus into an ointment of apples <note>original: *unguento de pomis* — This refers to "pomatum" or pomade, a scented ointment originally made using apples.</note>, and it will serve for anointing parts of the body to procure a fiery glow, but will the juice of apples therefore turn out to be Phosphorus? In the same way, will salt of urine exalt the sulfur of Mercury or of gold, so that an illuminating sulfur might be made from them? I know many have been in that error, and also the Englishman Starkey <note>George Starkey (1628–1665) was a prominent alchemist and physician who wrote under the name Eirenaeus Philalethes and was known for his work on the universal solvent called the "Alcahest."</note>, who thought the Alcahest <note>A hypothetical universal solvent sought by alchemists to break down substances into their primary components.</note> liquor could be prepared from urine. But this [light] is of a more sublime origin, along with its womb-brother, the Mercury of the Sages <note>original: *Sophorum Mercurio* — This is "Philosophical Mercury," a refined, spiritual substance distinct from common quicksilver used in the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

This quicksilver will shine with no less brilliance, except that its glow is more pale, while the other glows red <note>original: *rutilet* — This suggests a shimmering, golden-red light associated with the "soul" of gold.</note>. It is truly a delightful spectacle. The struggle of these two will be most pleasant to see. But I confess there is no one who can look upon this without being utterly terrified. Thus he spoke.*

But concerning the method itself, he adds nothing but what is utterly obscure, indeed deceptive, so that these words are merely without the "soul of things" <note>A phrase suggesting the text contains the outward form of a recipe without the essential chemical truth or "spirit" needed to make it work.</note>. Beccher’s reasoning regarding the preparation of Light-bearing Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius Luciferus* — A term for a mercurial substance that emits light, essentially a "mercurial phosphorus."</note> contains very subtle speculations founded upon chemical principles and drawn from the parables of the Hermeticists <note>Followers of Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>. There are four preparations of quicksilver <note>original: *argenti vivi* — Literally "living silver," the standard term for mercury.</note> (I speak according to the opinion of Beccher), and from each preparation, a Mercury of different perfection results. The first consists in **Essential Decomposition**, when a greater, more perfect, and thinner "leaf" <note>original: *folium* — In alchemical jargon, this refers to the subtle, essential part of a metal.</note> according to Basilian terms <note>Referring to the works attributed to Basil Valentine, a famous, likely pseudonymous, 15th-century alchemist.</note>—that is, a "golden opacity," namely gold or "physical sulfur"—is introduced into the quicksilver. For Mercury is nothing other than some metal reduced into a flux <note>original: *fluor* — A state of liquid flow or melting.</note> by the "mercurifying" first entity of salts. # DISCOURSE ON LIGHTS

<page-type>text</page-type>

*It is within mercury, says Helmont; because its seed and its fruit in the constitution of mercury are already one and the same mercury within mercury. Nor has nature known how to find a way of destruction in a thing so homogeneous, where the seed has become the fruit through a most perfect and equal union <note>original: "unione perfectiſſimâ & anaticâ" — "anatica" is a technical term meaning in equal parts or proportions.</note>. For nature cannot penetrate to divide where there is no knot or heterogeneity.* Therefore, let this play of subtle fantasy cease. The <term>Alkahest|The legendary universal solvent sought by alchemists, capable of reducing any substance to its primary matter.</term> cannot be prepared from common mercury through the separation of the metal, as I shall demonstrate in another place with more evidence. And if that mercurial entity exists elsewhere before it has assumed the metallic leaf <note>original: "folium metallicum" — here referring to the outward metallic form or shell of common mercury.</note>, as **Beccher** <note>Johann Joachim Beccher (1635–1682), an influential German chemist and physician.</note> himself admits in his preparation—and indeed a purely Virgin entity—what need is there to unravel common mercury into its principles, a task that is naturally impossible forever? Indeed, if mercury were divisible into different parts, the **chemical art** <note>original: "ars chymica" — here meaning the science of alchemy and transformation.</note> would not be true. Again, **Helmont** <note>Jean Baptiste van Helmont (1580–1644), a Flemish pioneer of chemistry and medicine.</note> states this elegantly:

### PART II. ON THE CAUSES OF PHOSPHORUS. 255

Whatever the preparation, it contains a most subtle phantasm, and is merely a true specter of Philosophy, not a real appearance in nature. **Beccher** <note>Johann Joachim Beccher (1635–1682), a German physician and alchemist known for his theory of "earths."</note> supposes that this **Virgin Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium istum Virgineum" — A hypothetical, pure form of mercury found in nature before it becomes "fixed" as a common metal.</note> in the mines seizes the arsenical sulfur of sea salt, and is thus established in a neutral state; it is no longer a "virgin," for it has already "married" the arsenical sulfur. Nor is it "mineral," because it has not yet been impregnated by any metal—seeing as by the touch of such a thing it is changed into common **quicksilver** <note>original: "vulgare hydrargyron"</note>. Instead, he calls it "meretricious" <note>original: "meretricium" — In alchemical terms, this describes a substance that has a "promiscuous" affinity or appetite to bond with any metal it touches.</note>, because it has an appetite for all metals, yet has not yet suffered a union with them. From this Mercury, disposed most closely toward turning into mercury, he thinks that **stinking solvent** <note>original: "menstruum illud fœtens"</note> is prepared, or that **stinking water of Hermes** <note>original: "aquam istam fœtidam Hermetis"</note>, about which there is such great rumor among the Philosophers—especially in **Lully** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan polymath. Alchemical texts attributed to him were highly influential in the 17th century.</note>, than whom no one has described this solvent more sincerely or openly.

I shall add a certain reality to Beccher’s "specter." This **Virgin Mercury** is nothing other than the **primary essence** <note>original: "primum ens"</note> of sea salt, which does not essentially differ from those saline-mercurial vapors <note>original: "halitibus istis salino-mercurialibus"</note>, or mineral **meteors** <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any natural phenomena in the air or earth, such as glowing vapors, lightning, or subterranean fumes.</note> flashing within and sometimes above the earth, which are in truth married to arsenical sulfur; for otherwise [they would not emit] the prime-material light of metals...

## CHAPTER V.

### *On the utility and use of Phosphorus substances.*

If knowledge were not a companion to the curiosity surrounding **Phosphorus** <term>Phosphorus | From the Greek for "light-bearer." In the 17th century, this referred not just to the chemical element, but to any substance—like the Bologna Stone or treated urine—that glowed in the dark.</term>, and if it possessed absolutely no utility, every discussion about them might seem vain. For who would judge a matter worthy of investigation if it bore no fruit at all? Therefore, some points regarding their use and utility must be subjoined here, which are perhaps not read or known by everyone. For phosphorus substances do not merely serve for the simple delight of the eyes, as **Potier** <note>Pierre Potier (lat. Petrus Poterius), a 17th-century French physician and chemist known for his medicinal preparations.</note> seems to have believed, but they can also be destined for a higher purpose. This is the goal which the most **illustrious Academy** <note>likely referring to the Academia Naturae Curiosorum (the Leopoldina), one of the oldest scientific societies in the world</note> also seems to have intended, and toward which, as far as I was able, I have attempted to aim in this exercise.

First of all, once the nature of Phosphorus is properly known, it kindles a clear light for perceiving the essence of light itself more clearly. Not that we believe, as the common folk do, that they truly burned and were **ever-shining** <note>original: "perennilucas"</note> for so many centuries because of some ignited **incombustible oil**; but rather, we think that light persisted in a far different manner, and indeed without actual fire. For when the nature of fire is considered, it is a contradiction for it to burn in a completely closed vessel with the air excluded—even if we assume, as must be supposed, that the fuel is provided by an **incombustible material**. Such material is unable to catch fire because its **fixity** <term>fixity | The quality of a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to heat.</term> and density prevent **rarefaction** <term>rarefaction | The process of a substance becoming less dense, such as a liquid turning into a gas, which was thought necessary for combustion.</term> and block the rapid motion of the **first element** <note>original: "primi elementi." In the physics of the time, this referred to the finest, most agitating particles of matter (often associated with Cartesian "subtle matter") necessary to sustain the heat and light of a flame.</note>, which is absolutely necessary for the natural existence and preservation of fire.

Numerous accounts of such lamps exist, but they are all quite imperfect, relying only on the claim that they burned while enclosed, but were extinguished once air was admitted.

# CHAPTER I.

## Proof that a Philosophical-Hermetic Phosphorus Exists.

<margin>Commentary on the *Gate of Ripley*, Chapter 1 <note>This refers to George Ripley’s (c. 1415–1490) famous alchemical work, *The Compound of Alchemy*, also known as the *Twelve Gates*.</note></margin>

This light shines upon only the rarest of craftsmen. The most ingenious Philaletha <term>Eirenaeus Philalethes: A pseudonym for a 17th-century alchemist, likely George Starkey, whose works were highly influential on Isaac Newton and Robert Boyle.</term> provides the reason:

> *Darkness, he says, possesses within itself the light of a "fool’s fire" <term>ignis fatuus: Literally "foolish fire," referring to phosphorescent swamp gas or the "will-o'-the-wisp"; used here to represent false or misleading knowledge.</term> by which its inhabitants think themselves marvelously enlightened... but once the light of nature reaches their stations, it reveals an utter gloom in which only an imaginary light once shone—just like the fool’s fire and that of fireflies <note>original: *lampyridum*</note>, which glimmers only in the dark. This [false light] nonetheless makes their eyes so sensitive that they neglect the writings by the light of nature’s lamp, nor do they look within, nor can they endure the light of the true lunar-stone <term>lunaria: While literally referring to the "moon-wort" plant, in this alchemical context it refers to a cooling, silver-like light or substance essential to the "Great Work."</term> of the wise. For any true light reveals their darkness. Yet their darkness cannot comprehend the light.*

Thus it is. Therefore, I have said it is necessary to provide here a certain torch for such people, which may illuminate somewhat the most obscure path to the hall of light. I will first demonstrate that light is found in the Philosophical subject, for that reason called *Lunaria* <term>Lunaria: Literally "moon-like" or "of the moon." In alchemy, this refers to a specific substance or plant that allegedly reflects the "light" of the work, often associated with the silver-making process.</term>; I shall show that a Hermetic Phosphorus exists. Since this is not granted to me through *a priori* reasoning <note>Reasoning based on theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note>, I will bring forward the authorities of the Adepts, and I will rely on their credibility; whoever wishes to render their credit weak should be careful not to inflict a great injury upon such excellent men. I will bring forward several opinions by which they intended to indicate this, and then their own experiences, which are accustomed to be the most proven of all proofs, and to surpass every syllogism.

I repeat now at last, toward the end, what I established at the beginning: that light is the form and essence of all things. It is composed of that **luminous sulfur of nature**, which the Philosophers also call the **simple fire of nature**, and which they maintain is nothing other than the **coagulated spirit of the Sun**. Although this spirit, in its universal or general undetermined state, is present everywhere—as we have demonstrated regarding air, water, and earth—it must nevertheless be sought in specific "elemented" subjects <term>Elemented subjects: Physical substances composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) in which the universal spirit is more concentrated and accessible.</term> in which, *according to Sendivogius, it exists but is not apparent until it pleases the craftsman.* <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636) was a Polish alchemist and physician who theorized that a "food of life" existed in the air.</note> It is, however, by far the most difficult task to choose those specific subjects of this **luminous spirit** <note>original: "spiritûs hujuſce lucidi"</note> without error—subjects of which nature recognizes only two. For **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a philosopher to whom many influential alchemical texts were attributed.</note> himself admits that every mineral is of a different kind, and one is better than another. For the student of **Physical Light** <term>Physical Light: In this context, the "Lux Physica" refers to the literal and spiritual light trapped within physical matter that the alchemist seeks to release.</term>, who can say how much darkness is produced everywhere on the **path of Hermes** <term>Path of Hermes: The "Hermetic" path refers to the secret processes of alchemy, named after the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus.</term> by ignorance of these specific materials?

Or rather, if you consider the matter exactly—looking at its nature rather than its quantity—it is found in one thing. ...emblematic ideas. To those students of truth, I permit whatever I have brought forward in this exercise concerning these three types of **Phosphorus** <note>original: *Phosphoris*. In this context, it refers to various "light-bearing" substances described throughout the text, both natural and alchemical.</note> to be investigated, believed, refuted, or corrected as they wish, provided they bring forth better, clearer, and truer proofs of light. If anyone, positioned in a clearer sphere of **Adept Light** <term>lucis Adeptæ</term> <note>Referring to the "Adept," a master who has successfully achieved the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note>, should recognize that I have not hit the intended mark in all things, let him remember that saying of the Great **Scaliger** to **Cardano**:

<margin>Exercise 131.</margin>
> *In the faint light of things we grope in the dark; in moderate light we are half-blind; in greater light we are blind; and in the greatest light, we are driven mad.* <note>original Latin: "In luce rerum tenui nos caligare, in mediocri cæcutire, in majori cæcos esse, in maximâ insanire." Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558) was a famous scholar who wrote a series of "Exercises" critiquing the polymath Girolamo Cardano.</note>

To the Divine Power and the Heavenly Light be immortal thanks for the illumination granted to me; may it furthermore, by the rays of its divine grace, turn away from us all darkness, blindness, and madness. To Him alone be honor and glory,

***

<margin>Anonymous Anthology on the Golden Tractate of Hermes, in the *Theatrum Chymicum*.</margin> <note>The *Theatrum Chymicum* (Chemical Theater) was a massive and influential compendium of alchemical writings published in the 17th century.</note>
> ->from whose light all light<-
> ->Shines forth; without whom bright things grow dark; from whom<-
> ->The shadows grow bright, and the image of unpleasant night vanishes.<- <note>original Latin: "cujus de lumine lumen / Omne micat, sine quo tenebrescunt lucida, de quo / Lucescunt tenebræ, atque inamœnæ noctis imago."</note>

->T H E   E N D.<-

- 302. line 7. for attentive <note>original: "attentis"</note> read woven together <note>original: "attextis"</note>.
- 305. line 5. read of multiplication <note>original: "multiplicationis"</note>.
- In the Index, read Night-shining <note>original: "Noctiluca"; a term used in this period to describe phosphorus or bioluminescent organisms.</note>.
